title: Understanding a dataset
summary: What one row stands for, reading and writing a data dictionary, and profiling an export with a few formulas before you trust it.
objectives: Say what one row of a dataset stands for, and why rows aren’t always orders.
Read and write a data dictionary: field, meaning, type, example.
Profile an export: rows, distinct keys, date range, blanks and categories.
List the questions a profile raises before analysis starts.

slides.h: Granularity: what one row stands for
p: Before any formula, ask: **what does one row stand for?** In Taraloom’s export one row is one product in an order, not one order.
The **grain** of a dataset is what one row stands for: an order line, a customer, a day.
Count rows and you count lines. Count **distinct OrderIDs** to count orders.
Averages need care too: “average order value” is revenue ÷ orders, not ÷ rows.
In real life: said “10,000 orders this year”. It was 10,000 order lines: 7,808 orders. A director spotted it before the meeting, but only just.

slides.h: Keys: the columns that name things
p: A **key** is a column that identifies something. Some keys are unique in a dataset; others repeat, and how they repeat tells you the grain.
The columns that are unique **together** are the row’s key: here OrderID + SKU.
Keys are what lookups and joins use in Module 3.
If the “unique” key repeats, you’ve found duplicates (Module 2).
In real life: counted patients by counting bill rows and reported 40% more patients than were admitted. One patient, many bills.

slides.h: A data dictionary says what each column means
p: A **data dictionary** lists every column with its meaning, type and an example. Write one for every dataset you receive, and ask about anything you can’t fill in.
The meaning is the hard part: is Amount before or after discount? With or without GST?
Ask the person who sent the data; don’t guess.
Keep it on a sheet in the workbook, so the next person has it too.
In real life: reported margins 18% too high: “Amount” in the export already included GST. The dictionary she wrote afterwards now says so in the first line.

check.q: An export has 240 rows and 184 distinct OrderIDs. What does one row stand for?
check.explain: More rows than orders means some orders take several rows: one row per product in the order.

why.0: Then rows and distinct orders would be equal.
why.1: Customers repeat across orders; the row isn’t a customer.

p: A **profile** is a short panel of facts about a dataset: how many rows, how many of each key, the date range, blanks and categories. It takes five minutes and saves days.
Every number in the profile is a formula, so it updates when a new export arrives.
Each surprise becomes a question to ask the sender.
Keep the profile next to the data, or on its own sheet.
In real life: profiled a “full year” of transactions and found the last date was 28 February. March was in a second file nobody had mentioned.

hl.label: 3 rows have no city: ask why

p: Six short formulas answer most profiling questions. You know every function already from C2.
COUNTA counts filled cells, so it undercounts if the column has blanks; ROWS counts every row.
UNIQUE on several columns finds distinct **combinations**.
Format date answers as dates, or MIN shows a number like 45749.
In real life: keeps these six formulas on a sheet called Profile and pastes each week’s export next to it. The panel tells her in seconds whether the week looks normal.

slides.h: Look at the values, not just the counts
p: List each category column’s values with **SORT(UNIQUE())** and look at the smallest and largest numbers. That’s where surprises hide.
Five channels where you expected three means spellings to standardise.
A negative quantity might be a return, or a typing mistake: ask.
A date in the future, or before the business started, is a red flag.
In real life: listed the units column with SORT(UNIQUE()) and found “kg”, “KG”, “Kg.” and “kgs”. Four spellings, one unit.

tasks.prompt: In **O2**, count the **rows of data** (order lines).
hints: Every row has an OrderID in column A.
ROWS counts the rows in a range; COUNTA counts filled cells.
OrderIDs repeat when an order has two products.

mistakes.msg: That counts every row. Wrap the column in UNIQUE first so each order counts once.

hints: Dates are numbers, so the first is the smallest.
The last date is the largest number.

tasks.prompt: In **O7**, count the rows with **no city**.
hints: There’s a function that counts empty cells.

tasks.prompt: In **O8**, show the average number of **rows per order**.
hints: Both are already in your panel.

tasks.prompt: In **Q2**, list each **channel** once, A to Z, with one formula.
hints: UNIQUE removes repeats; SORT puts them in order.

quiz.q: Rows per order is 1.30. What does that tell you?
options: On average an order has 1.3 products (rows)
quiz.explain: Rows ÷ distinct orders: some orders take two or three rows.

quiz.q: Which counts the rows in A2:A241 even if some cells are blank?
quiz.explain: ROWS counts rows whatever they hold. COUNTA skips blanks; COUNT only counts numbers.

quiz.q: Predict: MIN of a column of dates shows 45749. What do you do?
options: Format the cell as a date
quiz.explain: Dates are numbers; 45749 is 2 April 2025 once formatted as a date.

quiz.q: What belongs in a data dictionary?
options: Each field’s meaning, type and an example
quiz.explain: Meaning, type and example, plus anything surprising you learnt.

quiz.q: Which pair of columns is the key of an order line?
quiz.explain: Together they name exactly one row.

quiz.q: SORT(UNIQUE()) on Channel shows Instagram, insta, Marketplace, Website. What next?
options: Note it: “insta” needs standardising to Instagram before analysis
quiz.explain: Spelling variants are cleaning work (Module 2). Never delete rows to make a problem go away.

points: Know the **grain**: what one row stands for. Rows aren’t always orders.
Write a **data dictionary**: meaning, type and example for every column.
**Profile** with ROWS, COUNTA(UNIQUE()), MIN/MAX, COUNTBLANK and SORT(UNIQUE()).
